"Okay, then," she said, "you need to hear what I have to say."
He replied, "I'm listening."

"There's an old saying around here: 'If you need answers, go to Abel, and they'll sort it out.' We're a peaceful and loyal town. And you're over here trying to destroy one of Israel's most important cities. Why would you want to destroy what belongs to God?"

Joab shot back, "No way, you've got it all wrong. I'm not here to destroy anything, I swear! The problem is this one guy from the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba son of Bicri. He rebelled against King David. Just hand him over, only him, and we'll leave you alone."
The woman told Joab, "Deal. His head will be thrown over the wall to you."

The woman went and explained her plan to the whole city, and they did it. They cut off the head of Sheba son of Bicri and tossed it down to Joab. He blew the ram's horn, and all the soldiers packed up and went home. Joab then went back to the king in Jerusalem.

Joab was back in charge as the commander of Israel's entire army. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the Kerethites and Pelethites; Adoniram was over the labor crews; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the royal secretary; Sheva was the historian; Zadok and Abiathar were the priests; and Ira the Jairite was David's personal priest.

title: David's Crazy Famine & Giant Problems
paragraphs: Back in David's day, there was this crazy famine. It just wouldn't stop, like, for three whole years. So David finally hits up God and is like, 'Yo, what's the deal?' God tells him, 'It's because of Saul and his family. Remember when he went and totally wiped out the Gibeonites? Yeah, that's why.'

So David gets the Gibeonites together to talk. Quick backstory: the Gibeonites weren't actually Israelites. They were the last of the Amorites, and Israel had a treaty to protect them. But Saul, being extra for Israel and Judah's honor, tried to get rid of them anyway.
David asks the Gibeonites, 'What can I do for you guys? How can I make things right so you'll bless God's people and land again?'
The Gibeonites were like, 'We don't want money from Saul's family. And we're not about to start executing Israelites.'
But David was persistent, 'So what are you saying? What should I do?'
Then they told him, 'The guy who tried to erase us, who plotted to wipe us off the map? Well, give us seven of his sons. We'll execute them—hang them before God at Gibeah of Saul, the holy mountain.'
And David was like, 'All right. I'll hand them over to you.'

The king spared Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, because of the promise he and Jonathan made before God. But he took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had with Saul, and the five sons that Saul's daughter Merab had with Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite. He handed them over to the Gibeonites, who hanged all seven of them on the mountain before God. They all died together, right when the barley harvest was starting.

Rizpah, Aiah's daughter, took some rough cloth and made a spot for herself on a rock. She stayed there from the beginning of the harvest until the rains came, shooing away birds from the bodies during the day and wild animals at night.

Someone told David what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done. So he went and got the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the leaders of Jabesh Gilead (they had snatched their bodies from the town square in Beth Shan where the Philistines had hung them after striking them down at Gilboa). He gathered their remains and the bodies of the seven who were just hanged. They took the bodies back to the land of Benjamin and gave them a proper burial in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father.
They did everything the king ordered. After that, God started answering Israel's prayers for the land again.

War broke out again between the Philistines and Israel. David and his crew went down to fight, and David got super tired. Ishbi-Benob, a descendant of the giant Rapha, who had a spear that weighed almost eight pounds and was rocking all-new armor, was like, 'I'm gonna kill David.' But Abishai, Zeruiah's son, came in for the save, took down the Philistine, and killed him.
After that, David's men made him promise, 'You're not fighting on the front lines with us anymore! We can't risk the lamp of Israel getting snuffed out.'
Later, there was another fight with the Philistines at Gob. This time, Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, another one of Rapha's giant descendants.
In another battle at Gob, Elhanan son of Jaar, a weaver from Bethlehem, killed Goliath the Gittite, whose spear was as huge as a flagpole.

There was another fight in Gath. This time there was a giant who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—twenty-four in total! He was also a descendant of Rapha. He started dissing Israel, sso Jonathan son of Shimeah, David's nephew, killed him.
These four giants were all descendants of Rapha in Gath. And they all got taken out by David and his soldiers.

title: My God is My Ultimate Protector
paragraphs: So David sang this song to God after God saved him from all his enemies and from Saul.

God is my solid rock, my fortress, the one who rescues me. My God is the high cliff where I run for my life, hiding behind boulders, totally safe in my granite hideout. He's my mountain refuge, saving me from ruthless people.
I call out to God, who is worthy of all praise, and I'm saved from my enemies.
The waves of death were crashing over me; the floods of destruction terrified me. The ropes of the grave were wrapped around me; the traps of death were right in front of me.
In my distress, I called out to God; I cried to my God for help. From his temple, he heard my voice; my cry reached his ears.

The whole earth started shaking like crazy because God was furious. Smoke was pouring out of his nose, fire shooting out of his mouth. He ripped the sky open and came down, riding on the wind with dark storm clouds all around him. Then—boom—his brightness broke through like fireworks. God thundered from heaven and let loose his arrows and lightning, totally scattering the enemy. The bottom of the ocean got exposed, the earth's foundations laid bare, when God roared and unleashed his hurricane anger.

But God reached all the way down from the sky and grabbed me, pulling me out of that ocean of hate where I was drowning. My enemies were too strong for me and hit me when I was down, but God stuck by me. He set me down in a wide-open field and saved me—just because he loves me.

God put my life back together because I laid it all out before him. When I cleaned up my act, he gave me a fresh start. I've stayed on God's path and haven't blown him off. I check myself against his ways every day and try not to miss a thing. I've kept my hands clean, and God rewrote the story of my life when I opened my heart up to him.

God sticks by people who stick with him. He's straight with people who are straight with him, good to people who are good, and he outsmarts the shady ones. He lifts up the down-and-out but takes the stuck-up down a peg.

God, your light floods my path and drives out the darkness. With you I can smash through enemy lines and jump over walls. God's road is straight and smooth—every direction he gives is road-tested. Everyone who runs to him makes it.

Is there any god like God? He's the bedrock. He's the one who armed me and set me on the right path. Now I run like a deer, king of the mountain. He taught me how to fight—I can bend a bronze bow! He shields me with salvation and makes me feel ten feet tall. He gave me solid footing. When I chased my enemies, I caught them and didn't stop till they were done. I wiped them out. God armed me for battle and crushed the rebels. My enemies turned and ran. They cried for help but no one came; they yelled for God and got silence. I ground them to dust and swept them away like trash in the gutter. God rescued me from all the infighting and made me a leader of nations. People I'd never even heard of serve me now—they hear about me and surrender, coming out of their hideouts shaking.

Live, God! Blessings to my Rock, my towering Salvation-God! He set everything right for me and shut down everyone who talked back. He saved me from my enemies and pulled me away from violent bullies. That's why I'm thanking you, God, all over the world—that's why I'm singing songs about your name. God gives his king huge victories and shows endless love to his chosen one—to David and his kids, forever.

title: David's Last Words & His GOATed Squad
paragraphs: Alright, so check it out, these are David's final words. Like, his mic drop moment.
This is the speech of Jesse's son, the guy God literally lifted up to the top. The one the God of Jacob made king, and Israel's all-time favorite artist.

God's Spirit spoke through me, His words were right there on my tongue. The God of Israel, our Rock, told me, "Anyone who rules right and fair, who governs with respect for God, is like the first light of morning with no clouds, like fresh green grass after it rains." And honestly, that's how my rule has been. God made a solid promise with me, spelled it all out, and kept His word. My whole salvation, everything I wanted. But those who work for the devil? They're like thorns you just throw in the trash. Don't even try to touch them; use a rake or something. They're just gonna end up in a big bonfire.
Here's the list of David's best men, his top squad.
Josheb-Basshebeth, the Tahkemonite. He was the leader of the top Three. One time, he took on eight hundred guys with his spear and won. All in one day. Wild.

Next up of the elite Three was Eleazar, son of Dodai the Ahohite. He was with David when the Philistines were making fun of them at Pas Dammim. When the Philistines got ready for battle, the Israelite army bounced. But Eleazar stood his ground and just started wrecking Philistines left and right until he was totally wiped. But he never dropped his sword. That was a huge win for God that day. The rest of the army came back, but all they had to do was clean up the mess.

Shammah son of Agee the Hararite was the third of the Three. The Philistines had gathered for a fight at Lehi, in a field full of lentils. The Israelites ran away from the Philistines, but Shammah stood his ground in the middle of the field, defended it, and beat the Philistines. Another massive W for God.

One time during harvest, the Three left the Thirty and met up with David at the Cave of Adullam. A group of Philistines had set up camp in the Valley of Rephaim. While David was hiding in the cave, the Philistines had their main camp in Bethlehem. David was suddenly craving something and said, "Man, I'd love a drink of water from the well at the gate of Bethlehem." So the Three snuck through the Philistine lines, got water from the well in Bethlehem, and brought it back to David. But David wouldn't drink it. He poured it out as an offering to God, saying, "No way, God, I can't drink this. This isn't just water, it's their life-blood—they risked their lives to get it." So David refused to drink it.
This is the kind of stuff the Three did.

Abishai, brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was the leader of the Thirty. He got famous for killing three hundred guys with his spear, but he wasn't on the same level as the Three. He was the most respected of the Thirty and their captain, but he never made it into the top Three.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada from Kabzeel was a tough guy who did a lot of cool stuff. He once killed two lion cubs in Moab. Another time, on a snowy day, he went down into a pit and killed a lion. He also killed a huge Egyptian guy. The Egyptian had a spear, and Benaiah went up against him with just a walking stick. He snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.

These are the things Benaiah son of Jehoiada is known for. But he also never got ranked with the Three. He was super respected among the Thirty, but never made it into the Three. David made him his personal bodyguard.
"The Thirty" were:

Thirty-seven in total.

title: David's BIG Mistake & The Plague That Wrecked Israel
paragraphs: So, God was seriously ticked off at Israel again. He decided to test David and basically whispered in his ear, 'Yo, go count everyone in Israel and Judah.' So David, probably not thinking it through, tells his top general Joab, 'Alright, go do a headcount of all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba. I wanna see the numbers.'
But Joab was like, 'Bro, are you for real? May God make us a hundred times bigger, for sure, but why are you doing this? This is a bad look.'

But David wouldn't back down. He was like, 'Just do it.' So Joab and his crew had to bounce and start the census. They crossed the Jordan and started with Aroer and the town in the canyon of the Gadites near Jazer, went through Gilead, passed Hermon, then on to Dan but detoured around Sidon. They covered Fort Tyre and all the Hivite and Canaanite cities, and finally reached the Negev of Judah at Beersheba. The whole road trip took nine months and twenty days. When they got back to Jerusalem, Joab gave David the stats: 800,000 guys ready to fight in Israel, and 500,000 in Judah. That's a lot of dudes.
But then it hit David. He felt super guilty for counting everyone, like he was trusting numbers instead of God. He prayed, 'God, I messed up, big time. That was so dumb of me. Please forgive me.'
The next morning, God had already hit up his prophet Gad with a message for David. 'Go tell David this,' God said. 'I've got three punishments in mind. He gets to pick one, and I'll make it happen.'

Gad went to David and laid it out: 'You want three years of famine? Or three months of running for your life from your enemies? Or how about a three-day plague across the country? You need to decide. What should I tell God?'
David told Gad, 'Man, those are all horrible choices. But I'd rather be punished by God, because he's merciful, than be at the mercy of people.'

So God sent a plague that lasted from morning till evening. It was a total disaster. From Dan to Beersheba, 70,000 people died. But just as the angel was about to wreck Jerusalem, God was like, 'Okay, that's enough. Stop.'

The angel of God was at the threshing floor of a guy named Araunah the Jebusite. David looked up and saw the angel just hanging there between heaven and earth, with a sword out, ready to strike Jerusalem. David and the elders just fell to the ground, praying and freaking out.

When David saw the angel about to destroy everyone, he prayed, 'No, please! I'm the one who messed up. I'm the shepherd who did wrong. But these people are like innocent sheep, what did they do? Punish me and my family instead.'
That same day, Gad came to David and said, 'Go build an altar to God on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.' So David did what Gad said, just like God told him to.
Araunah saw the king and his guys coming over, so he went out and bowed down. 'My king, what brings you here?' he asked.
'I need to buy your threshing floor,' David said. 'I've got to build an altar to God here to stop this plague.'

Araunah was like, 'Oh, dude, just take it. Take whatever you want for the sacrifice. Here's an ox, and you can use the wooden yokes for firewood. It's all yours, on the house! And I hope your God blesses you.'
But the king said to Araunah, 'Nah, I have to buy it from you. I'm not going to offer God a sacrifice that cost me nothing.'
So David bought the threshing floor and the ox for fifty shekels of silver. He built an altar to God right there and made sacrifices. God heard their prayers, and the plague finally stopped.
